Iranians face arduous journeys as US sanctions ground planes. TEHRAN: Flying out of Iran has long required patience in the face of restrictions and delays, but new US sanctions have grounded flights at short notice and left war-weary travelers feeling trapped as they try to leave the country. Lebanese Forces chief says Hezbollah arms prolong Israeli presence in the south. LONDON: Lebanese Forces leader Samir Geagea accused Hezbollah on Monday of helping prolong Israel’s military presence in south Lebanon, saying the group’s refusal to disarm had prevented the Lebanese state from securing an Israeli withdrawal. Geagea made the comments in a statement responding to remarks by Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem, who said the group would not surrender its weapons and blamed Israel for Lebanon’s crisis. Cholera and measles threaten displaced in Yemen after renewed fighting uproots 142,000, UN warns. NEW YORK CITY: Overcrowded displacement sites in war-torn Yemen are increasing the risk of deadly cholera and measles outbreaks, the UN warned on Monday, as the recent escalation in fighting has driven another 142,000 people from their homes and pushed the country’s fragile health system to the brink. Israeli drones and fighter jets violate Lebanese airspace 143 times in 3 days, UN peacekeepers say. NEW YORK CITY: Israeli drones, fighter aircraft and helicopters violated Lebanese airspace 143 times over the weekend, UN peacekeepers in southern Lebanon reported. No rocket or artillery fire from Hezbollah or other armed groups was detected during that time. The UN Interim Force in Lebanon recorded the violations between Friday and Sunday, Stephane Dujarric, the spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told reporters in New York on Monday. UAE urges diplomacy, stronger international action on Gaza and regional crises at UN. LONDON: The UAE has called for greater reliance on diplomacy, dialogue and mediation to address global conflicts, while urging the international community to take concrete action to end the war in Gaza and address threats to regional maritime security. Addressing the UN General Assembly on Monday, UAE Minister of State Khalifa Shaheen Al-Marar said his country rejects the unlawful use or threat of force and coercion, stressing respect for state sovereignty, international law and the UN Charter.

Trump denies offering to sell arms to China's Xi. WASHINGTON: Donald Trump on Monday denied asking Xi Jinping if he would like to buy American weapons, after the US ambassador to Beijing said the US president made the offer to his Chinese counterpart. "I've never heard of that one," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked about the comments made by envoy David Purdue. 'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide Submitted by Anuradha Bhasin on Wed, 09/23/2026 - 11:36 The real danger isn't in how these lethal technologies, including pellet guns, are exported and shared; the greater peril is in the precedent their use against civilian protesters sets Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters wave national flags a day after the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in Mumbai, India, 26 July 2026 (Punit Paranjape/AFP) On In July 2026, Amnesty International published a report Made in India: the supply of weapons and munitions to Israel . It found India shipped hundreds of thousands of weapon parts and munitions components to Israel throughout its Gaza offensive, and it warned the exports carry a " substantial risk " of contributing to what it calls Israel's " ongoing genocide ". The real danger isn't only in how these lethal technologies are exported and shared. The greater peril is in the wrong precedent their use against civilians sets. A telling example is the use of pellet guns by police in Delhi to control a student’s march to the Indian parliament in protest against an examination leak scam, which injured at least 10 civilians , including a young man who may lose his vision forever. The journey of the use of pellet guns for crowd control from Kashmir to New Delhi reminds us that any battleground is always a testing ground. What gets legitimised in one place does not stay there. India introduced pellet guns in 2010 in Kashmir and framed it as a "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" weapon for crowd control. Between 2010 and 2019, 24 people were killed. Most casualties happened after their widespread use to control violent protests following the death of militant commander Burhan Wani , who was killed in an encounter in 2016. Between July 2016 and February 2019, metal pellets killed 18 people, blinded 139, and resulted in 2,942 injuries , of which 1,459 were serious eye injuries. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); A pellet gun is a .12-bore pump-action shotgun, normally used in bird hunting , that fires a cartridge loaded with several hundred metal pellets that disperse over a wide area rather than travelling as a single projectile. Each cartridge holds up to several hundred small pellets. On firing, the pellets scatter outward in a wide spray at about 100-150 metres per second. Because of this spread, one shot can strike multiple people in a crowd at once. In short, it doesn’t choose its target. It can hit anyone within that range. The enormous scale of injuries, even deaths, caused by pellets in Kashmir and the people they hit - a girl sitting by her window, a baby in her mother’s arms - made no distinction between allegedly violent protesters and those who just happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong moment. Opening old wounds The brutality of the pellet guns cannot be fully comprehended without understanding how the lives of the majority of the victims are scarred forever. Despite the "less-lethal" tag, the pellets are sharp enough to pierce the skin and stay embedded in the body , causing permanent pain in some cases. On occasion, they have caused permanent blindness. The psychological wounds they inflict are irreparable. There have also been cases of injuries resulting in deaths . Yet, the use of pellet guns in Kashmir was justified under a manufactured broad consensus built entirely through a security prism. The state embraced the weapon, framing it as "non-lethal", despite documentary evidence of hundreds blinded, scores killed, and many others permanently disabled. It invited no uproar or outrage. This nationwide tendency to see Kashmir as a state of exception has also encouraged a shameful mocking of its victims - the latest example being the forthcoming Bollywood film Chauhaan . It was used with the bland justification: terrorism, national security. This, even as there is no documentary evidence of the weapon ever being used against insurgents - only on civilian protesters. A security doctrine, borrowed from international playbooks, and built for a region on the pretext of insurgency, is now being exported. History of violence Before its use in Delhi, pellet guns were used during the farmers’ protest and in Manipur . Their use in Delhi against protesting students evoked nationwide outrage, with the framing "they were students, not terrorists’". That framing never extends to the community the national imagination has already conflated with terrorists - Kashmir, Manipur and Punjab (whose farmers led the protests). The presumption of innocence isn't universal. It is assigned by identity. Lethal weapon: How Bollywood's 'Chauhaan' trivialises the suffering of Kashmiris maimed by Indian forces Read More » Far more problematic is the state response that is still relying on old tactics of skirting questions about pellet injuries. It has moved from denial to deflection but no accountability . As opposition leaders led by Congress, a party that ironically introduced pellet guns in 2010, are uniting and demanding answers to who ordered the pellet guns and why, India’s home minister Amit Shah has refused to attend parliament. Zero accountability automatically translates to a continuum of use of pellet guns or other weapons framed as "non-lethal’". In Kashmir, there is a documented record of young men killed when tear gas shells were directly aimed at their upper bodies in 2010. Even the Supreme Court has refused a total ban on the use of pellet guns and has deflected the question to examining the gaps between standard operating procedures and realities on the ground. The debate on whether lethal weapons can be used for crowd control is incomplete if restricted to these issues. The debate also needs to take into account the impact of weapons that are projected as "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" but kill people nonetheless. It needs to weigh up the fact that a bad precedent travels from one geography to another and beyond borders. Lethal export Pellet guns have already travelled the globe. The United Kingdom is the first known country to have deployed shotguns with rubber and plastic pellets during the Troubles , the 30-year violent conflict in Northern Ireland, and inspired the United States police to adopt similar versions of the weapon for crowd control. Pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged Pellet guns, along with other so-called "non-lethal" weapons, have been used with impunity in Palestine . Whether India borrowed this method of repression from Israel or not, the list of countries now using it to target their own citizens is growing. In Chile in 2019, 230 people lost their vision. Bangladesh used it in 2024, killing 22 student protesters and blinding 400. They were used in the recent Iran protests, with at least 74 documented cases of pellet injuries in vital parts of the body. A man’s lung was damaged by 174 pellets tightly packed inside his right chest cavity. The pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged. Nuclear strikes may be a rare exception, but there are enough examples, like the use of white phosphorous and drone air strikes that reveal a brutal truth: what is used in one place doesn’t stay there; it travels wherever the next authority wants the same cover of impunity. Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner Submitted by Oscar Rickett on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 07:00 Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali was extradited from Serbia and has been in Bahrain's Jau Prison since 2022 Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali has been held in Jau Prison since he was deported from Serbia in January 2022 (ADHRB) Off The Council of Europe has called on Serbia to implement a European Court of Human Rights judgement, which held that the Balkan country had violated the European Convention on Human Rights when it extradited a Bahraini activist seeking asylum. Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali travelled to Serbia to seek asylum in November 2021 but was arrested by authorities there based on an Interpol red notice, which Ali’s lawyers say was unlawfully issued. The European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure in January 2022 calling on Serbian authorities to refrain from extraditing Ali pending more information and particularly given the risk of torture or ill-treatment if he was returned. Three days later, campaigners say a private plane, chartered by United Arab Emirates -based Royal Jet Airlines, took Ali to Bahrain . Ever since then the activist, who fled Bahrain in 2011 and then lived in Iran before travelling to Serbia, has been held in Bahrain’s Jau Prison on two life sentences. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Inside the prison, Ali says he has been beaten, denied medical treatment, had his faith insulted and held in solitary confinement. According to a recent call with fellow activists, a transcript of which was seen by Middle East Eye, Ali is currently being held in the prison’s Building Two, which houses violent offenders and those on serious drug charges. Inside the building, the activist says these prisoners - acting on instruction from prison guards - beat and abuse him, creating a climate of fear that never lifts. European ruling on Serbia In March 2025, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Serbia had violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) by extraditing Ali in defiance of an interim court block. Article 3 of the convention safeguards against torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The Serbian courts violated this when they failed to examine Ali’s complaint that he would face ill-treatment if sent back to Bahrain. He is stuck in a severely overcrowded cell, has repeatedly had to resort to hunger strikes just to secure basic rights, and has been in and out of solitary confinement - Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, Bird The ECHR ordered Serbia to pay 9,800 euros ($11,100), plus any tax chargeable and interest in the event of a default in payment. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers says that, since the judgement, Serbia has placed a sum of money for Ali in a deposit account in a domestic court. However, the committee acknowledged his lawyers’ argument that there are “difficulties in complying with the conditions for the release of the funds given the exceptional nature of [Ali’s] situation” in Jau Prison. The Council of Europe has said that Serbia should “co-operate with [Ali’s] representatives and the Secretariat to find solutions to enable the release of funds to take place without delay”. Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, director of advocacy at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (Bird), told MEE that he had also been held in Building Two at Jau Prison, and that talking to Ali recently had brought back, in vivid detail, the suffering he had experienced there. “It was very hard to hear Ahmed describing to me the degrading conditions he is living in at Jau Prison. He is stuck in a severely overcrowded cell, has repeatedly had to resort to hunger strikes just to secure basic rights, and has been in and out of solitary confinement,” Alwadaei said. “This decision is an important reminder that Serbia cannot simply take Bahrain’s assurances at face value. It must face the reality of what happened after Ahmed’s unlawful extradition and do everything it can to protect him.” (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Political prisoners in Bahrain Last year, Amnesty said that an estimated 322 political prisoners remained arbitrarily detained in Bahrain. Bahrain Grand Prix: Twenty years of dissent and sportswashing Read More » In the wake of the Arab Spring uprising of 2011, thousands of Bahrainis – mostly from the Sunni-ruled kingdom’s majority Shia population – were arrested and thrown in prison. In 2024, Bahrain granted 1,500 prisoners royal pardons, and other similar moves have followed, but, according to Amnesty, the government continues to “suppress the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, including through arbitrary detention and prosecutions”. The US - Israeli war on Iran has also resulted in a new crackdown from Bahraini authorities, including stripping citizenship from those expressing anything deemed to be supportive of Iran, which has struck targets inside Bahrain. In his recent call from Jau Prison, Ali described being kept in an overcrowded cell in which half the inmates had to sleep on the floor and in which a lack of ventilation resulted in “suffocating” conditions. In July, he says he was badly beaten, and he remains “under threat at any moment” from the same “gang”. The toilet and washing facilities are unsanitary, he said, with prisoners relying on a hose to wash themselves and overflowing drains. INFRASTRUCTURE: THE LAST STOP. Most days, I leave my office at around 5pm, after which it takes roughly half an hour at the bus stop for my bus to arrive. The bus ride itself takes another hour to ninety minutes. From there, it is a 15-minute walk to my house in the Gulistan-i-Johar area of Karachi. The first challenge is to cross the poorly-lit, forever-under-construction University Road, with cars and motorcycles — often without headlights — racing through the operational service lanes. At the end of a long and arduous day, walking home from the bus stop, I must not only be wary of speeding vehicles, but also of criminals, opportunistic harassers and serial stalkers. Exacerbating this daily grind are hazards such as flooded roads — after rainfall or otherwise — where speeding vehicles may splash pedestrians, leaving them wet, exposed and helpless. What may seem like a minor inconvenience to a driver can become a deeply uncomfortable and humiliating moment for a pedestrian. These experiences led me to ask other women about their journeys. Those who took part in this informal survey use different modes of public transportation, including mini-buses, qingchis, electric buses, and other informal transport services. Their backgrounds and experiences vary, depending on factors such as their occupation, age, income, the areas they travel to and the time of day. They include people working in offices, banks, schools, hospitals, shops and factories, while others are domestic workers employed in private homes. Their stories reveal how concerns about safety persist throughout the journey — and do not end when women get off public transport. Long waits, overcrowded buses and unsafe infrastructure are only part of the daily commute for Karachi’s working women. Often, the most difficult stretch for them begins after they get off public transport WALKING BACK HOME One recurring concern expressed by women was their safety after getting off public transport and walking from the last stop to their homes. For many women, the walk takes between five and 10 minutes. Although public transport takes them to the last stop, the final walk home often feels unsafe, particularly during the evening or at night. Two women told me they had been hit by a motorbike without headlights. Another, a physiotherapist, told me she had been robbed of her cellphone while walking from the stop to her home in the Gulshan-i-Iqbal area. Equally challenging is the prospect of crossing a pedestrian bridge. These bridges are often poorly maintained and not well-lit, making them unsafe, especially after sunset. Some women said they had encountered people who use drugs on or around such bridges, making them feel unsafe. At least one passenger, an employee at a private hospital, told me that she faced harassment while crossing a pedestrian bridge. In addition, large advertising billboards frequently obstruct visibility, creating hidden spaces where pedestrians cannot easily see who is nearby. As a result, many women avoid pedestrian bridges altogether and choose to cross busy roads, despite the risk of being hit by traffic. Even walking short distances in extreme heat can be physically exhausting, while heavy rainfall often floods the streets and conceals open manholes and damaged roads. As a result, women fear falling into uncovered manholes or being injured while walking through waterlogged streets. A woman shared that, while walking to the bus stop to pick up her daughter, she fell into an uncovered manhole, suffering serious injuries. She says the construction site had no warning signs, safety barriers or adequate lighting to alert pedestrians to the danger. FINDING ALTERNATIVES A group of women working at a garment packaging factory explained that they are fortunate to live in the same neighbourhood and work at the same factory, allowing them to travel together each day. They use mini-buses for their daily commute, and their homes are about a 20-minute walk from the last stop. Instead of walking, the women collectively hire a rickshaw to cover the final part of their journey. Another group, also working at a factory, explained that they rarely travel alone after work. Factory transport drops them on main roads and they travel the last leg of their journey by themselves. They leave the factory in groups and often get lifts from Mazda drivers and loaders who live in the same neighbourhood or along the same route. Such informal support networks help reduce transport costs while also providing a greater sense of security during the last stage of their commute. One university student told me that she uses a bike-hailing service to get home after getting off the bus because it is more affordable than a rickshaw. She explained that this option allows her to reach home while keeping her transportation costs low. But not everyone can afford this. Women from low-income households say that financial constraints — the additional fare of a rickshaw, for instance — limit their options in the final stage of their daily commute. They get off at the main road and walk the remaining distance to their homes. Their experiences demonstrate how economic inequality directly influences personal safety and mobility. The inability to afford last-mile transport can force women to choose between financial necessity and personal security. SAFETY IN NUMBERS Travelling together allows the women to look out for one another, particularly when walking from the last stop to their homes or passing through poorly lit and isolated areas. It also gives women an opportunity to form unexpected connections. The same sense of connection emerged during my own daily trips on public transport. I have made quite a few friends, particularly among those using the same route regularly. We gradually became familiar with each other and, over time, repeated encounters gradually turned into friendships, built on familiarity, trust and mutual support. Most of the women I spoke to describe these friendships as an important source of social and psychological support, helping to reduce feelings of isolation, anxiety and vulnerability while commuting. In this way, the bus stop also becomes more than a waiting space — it also serves as a place where solidarity and community are formed among women navigating the city’s public transport system. These everyday choices show how closely safety, mobility and economic inequality are intertwined. For many women, the commute does not end when they step off a bus or qingchi; negotiating the final stretch home is itself a daily calculation of cost, safety and convenience. The writer is a visual artist and works as a research assistant with architect Arif Hasan Published in Dawn, EOS, September 27th, 2026

US delegation meets CDF Munir, acknowledges Pakistan's 'longstanding role, sacrifices' during Afghan war. A delegation of America’s Afghanistan War Commission called on Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir on Monday and acknowledged Pakistan’s “longstanding role and sacrifices during the conflict in Afghanistan”, according to the military’s media affairs wings. The visiting delegation also appreciated Pakistan’s continued contribution to regional peace and stability, the Inter-Services Public Relations said in a statement. The delegation, led by its co-chairs, Shamila N. Chaudhary and Dr Colin F Jackson, met CDF Munir at General Headquarters (GHQ) in Rawalpindi. “The delegation is undertaking a review of the United States’ 20-year engagement in Afghanistan,” the statement said, adding that its discussion with the military chief covered topics including “Pakistan’s support, the regional security environment and developments in Afghanistan, with focus on perspectives relevant to the commission’s work”. For his part, CDF Munir shared Pakistan’s perspective on the security dynamics that shaped the conflict, also highlighting the challenges the country faced during the prolonged US engagement in Afghanistan. The ISPR statement added that he highlighted the need to incorporate a regional perspective, as well as Pakistan’s experience in assessing the strategic, diplomatic and operational dimensions of the conflict. The US Congress established the Afghanistan War Commission in 2021 as an independent body to review US decisions pertaining to the war in Afghanistan from June 2001 to August 2021, according to the commission’s website . US forces had withdrawn from Afghanistan in Aug 2021, ending a 20-year war. The withdrawal was completed a minute before midnight on Aug 30, 2021. The US had launched a military intervention in Afghanistan following the Sept 11, 2001, attacks, ushering in two decades of conflict in which civilians suffered widespread violence and abuses. Some 800,000 US servicemembers served in Afghanistan during this period. During the war, 2,238 US servicemembers died and nearly 21,000 were wounded. Meanwhile, over 40,000 civilians were killed and 77,000 wounded in attacks by Taliban insurgents, the Islamic State (IS) group, and in operations by the armed forces of the Afghan Republic or the international coalition led by the US, according to the United Nations mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA). Independent estimates put the total number of Afghan security forces and civilians killed at more than 100,000. A detailed report in The Wall Street Journal in 2022 showed that since Sept 11, 2001, US military outsourcing had pushed up Pentagon spending to $14 trillion. One-third to half of that sum went to contractors.

CM Afridi strikes defiant tone as federal ministers rail against KP govt's counter-terror fight. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Monday struck a defiant tone and again panned the Centre’s counterterrorism policy as federal ministers railed against his government’s efforts to combat terrorism. Afridi, who was elected as the KP CM in October 2025, has repeatedly voiced his opposition to the federal government’s policies on counterterrorism and Afghanistan. Earlier in the day, Kashmir affairs and frontier regions minister Amir Muqam held a press conference in Peshawar, where he slammed the PTI and Afridi for focusing on the party’s planned long march rather than the security challenges that KP was facing. Later, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, during a press briefing in Islamabad, highlighted flaws in the KP government’s “leadership” and use of resources to fight terrorism. This was followed by another press conference in Peshawar, where the prime minister’s coordinator to KP, Ikhtiar Wali Khan, and MNA Samar Haroon Bilour presented a white paper on the KP government’s “failure” to equip police with sophisticated weapons. Meanwhile, addressing a meeting regarding law and order in Peshawar, the KP CM stressed that merely providing resources to the police would not solve the problem until there was a policy shift. “We repeatedly stated that the state’s current policy was flawed. The blood of our Pakhtuns will flow again,” Afridi said, regretting that federal ministers “dismissed our repeated warnings as propaganda and lies”. The chief minister highlighted that he had been consistently calling for a change to the “failed policy of 22 years”. The PTI leader declared he would not back down from his stance over threats of imposition of governor’s rule or a state of emergency. Afridi called for a new counterterrorism policy to be formulated that took all stakeholders into confidence, including the provincial government, administration and police. He contended that if the new policy was implemented as proposed, peace could be restored in KP within 100 days — “yet no one is willing to listen”. “Some people act as if they know it all and are unwilling to listen to the stakeholders of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa,” he said. “Where is the country being led? Is the blood of our people so cheap that it should be sacrificed for the sake of politics?” CM Afridi also defended his government’s performance, recalling that it had diverted Rs35 billion from the development budget to the police force, doubling its allocation. He added that the Special Branch was being stabilised and modern weaponry and essential gear were being provided to the police force. The KP CM went on to accuse the federal government of adopting a “dual-standard policy”: “one for the favourites and another for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa”, terming this unacceptable. He again expressed concern over Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s comments that the other three provinces posed a threat rather than India, noting that she was contradicting the state’s stance that New Delhi had a role in sponsoring terrorism in Pakistan. “Federal ministers label the residents of KP as terrorists and savages; they are forgiven because they are favourites … no action is taken against them,” the PTI leader said. Azam Tarar says governor’s rule or emergency can happen Meanwhile, calls from federal representatives for imposing governor’s rule or an emergency in KP intensified, with Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar saying that such a move could be made if required. “If such conditions, where the constitution demands governor’s rule to be implemented or an emergency declared, are there or they arise, it can and will definitely happen,” he told Geo News . “If the mechanism in the constitution requires it, all these things will happen,” Azam said. In his media talk at Peshawar Press Club, Muqam said “all conditions” required by the law for imposing governor’s rule existed. Criticising Afridi’s governance, Muqam asserted that his “CM-ship would not continue and no one will be able to save him”. “Afridi sahib , be ready, you will be behind bars. You will be held accountable for the loot and plundering you have done,” the minister said. He criticised the PTI’s alleged lack of concern regarding the security challenges, contending that the party did not have enough public support. The federal minister described the Afridi-led provincial government as a complete failure on all fronts, claiming that it had neglected public welfare and that corruption was widespread in KP. Muqam further said that PTI leaders were conducting political activities across the country and did not appear to have any fear of terrorist attacks, even as other parties’ leaders faced such threats. Separately, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi held a meeting with Muqam to discuss the deteriorating law and order situation in the province and political developments, state-run APP reported . NA Standing Committee on Defence Chairman Fatihullah Khan Miankhel, National Democratic Movement (NDM) chief Mohsin Dawar, PPP Parliamentary Leader in KP Assembly Ahmad Kundi and MPA Sobia Khan were among those present. The participants exchanged views on the prevailing security situation, political uncertainty and other issues, and “deliberated on a number of proposals”, the APP report said. The leaders expressed serious concern over the rising incidents of insecurity in the province and termed the worsening situation a result of what they described as the provincial government’s failure to maintain law and order. Speaking to the media, Kundi warned the PTI government not to “force the Centre” to impose governor’s rule and urged it to further postpone its long march currently set for Oct 4 . Kundi said that in his opinion, governor’s rule could be imposed if the federal government deemed it necessary “to save the province”. “Fire is raging here,” he said while speaking on the province’s security situation. “I advise the provincial government to postpone their long march due to the law and order situation, call all stakeholders and political parties to discuss peace in the province, and fight terrorism on the frontline.” He contended that the PTI wanted to march on Islamabad and “spread chaos” even when terrorist incidents in KP were claiming people’s lives. Afridi responds to ‘white paper’ on KP govt In a post on X in the evening, CM Afridi asserted that the KP police and the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) were “extremely capable and equipped with modern weapons”. He appeared to be specifically responding to Wali’s allegations, sharing a screenshot from the latter’s press conference earlier. According to state broadcaster Radio Pakistan , the PML-N’s KP chapter issued a white paper on the provincial government’s performance. Pictures of the white paper’s cover shared by Wali and Bilour said the document pertained to the KP government’s “misgovernance during past one year” — since Afridi came to power. The PML-N leaders said over Rs800bn had been given to KP for counterterrorism efforts, but the provincial government had miserably failed to equip the police with much-needed sophisticated weapons and equipment. Giving a presentation, Wali said the KP CTD had only nine M4 rifles and 11 night vision devices for the entire province. “Bulletproof vehicles provided by the Centre were returned with arrogance and mockery, and today the province has just 17 vehicles. In contrast, Punjab has 76, and even a low-budget province like Balochistan has 42 bulletproof vehicles.” The PM’s coordinator said the number of police personnel martyred between January and June in 2025 rose by almost 94 per cent in the same period this year. Similarly, injuries to police personnel rose 108pc during the period, while terrorist attacks between January and September 2026 increased by 33pc compared to the same period in 2025. Speaking alongside him, Bilour highlighted that CM Afridi held his first meeting of the provincial apex committee in February , 112 days after taking oath. She particularly pointed out that Afridi focused a Sept 21 media talk, held just three days after the Kohat attack, on the PTI’s long march plans and dismissed a journalist’s question on the province’s situation. The PML-N leaders further alleged that the Afridi-led government has failed to curb the spread of drugs. According to his post, Afridi saw a conspiracy for an attack, which he described as an attempt to prove that KP police and CTD were weak. “Is the PML-N seeing KP as a testing ground and planning a major move?” he questioned. He alleged that Heavy Industries Taxila, which operates under the Centre, “is deliberately slowing down the delivery of the supplies despite payment by the provincial government”. The chief minister added that a payment had been made for weapons provided to the KP police but “other supplies are not being delivered despite the payment”. He warned of a strong response to any attempt at an “adventure”. ‘KP’s incompetent leadership’ In Islamabad, the state minister for interior said the PTI-led KP government had not made adequate efforts to combat terrorism. He noted that a political leadership could “provide three things in the fight against terrorism: leadership, resources and powers”. Chaudhry contended that the provincial administration in KP — where the PTI has been in power since 2013 — “did not provide leadership to the security forces over the past 14 years”. The interior official accused the PTI-led government of “creating space” for terrorists. “If Pakistan is burning in the fire of terrorism, it is because of KP’s incompetent leadership,” he maintained. Chaudhry then noted that it was the provincial government’s responsibility to allocate funds for counter-terrorism in the budget. “[Then], why did you not provide the resources?” he asked, adding that CTD was still not functional in the entire province. “Your forces cannot fight unarmed. You do not have bulletproof jackets, cars, training, CTD, Safe City [project], or a forensic lab,” he said, claiming that Safe City projects had been completed on the tehsil level as well in Punjab. The state minister sought accountability from KP over the usage of even 1pc of the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award, which he said amounted to Rs800bn. Chaudhry pointed out that Afridi and his information minister did not attend the funeral prayers of the victims of the Sept 18 Kohat blast , but were rather “busy in their street movement or other matters”. He recalled that the KP CM held a “very lengthy” press conference in Dera Ismail Khan in the wake of Saturday’s suicide blast , which claimed 12 lives. “Why did they not condemn Afghanistan? Why do you have a soft attitude on Afghanistan? Why do you deliberately employ such ambiguity and demeanour, and do not openly condemn or name the real enemy or from where these proxies operate?” he asked. Chaudhry reiterated his criticism of the recent KP Police Act , which has been proposed to replace a 2017 version and is aimed at curtailing the powers of the provincial inspector general (IG). He also responded to PTI’s allegation that the party had not been included in discussions about war on terrorism, saying that the party leadership did not show up to meetings when invited. “You come to Islamabad to demand NFC funds , but your CM does not show up for anti-terrorism meetings,” Chaudhry said. Speaking alongside him, Tarar said PTI had not taken ownership of the fight against terrorism, again terming the party as the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan’s (TTP) “B team”. He alleged that PTI had facilitated terrorists in its over 12 years of governing KP and that it was not condemning them as it “suits PTI’s financial interests”. “Sohail Afridi organised a ceremony and two Afghans did not stand up to pay respect to the national anthem. If I was there, I would have dealt with them right then and there. I would have banned them,” Tarar said. Such an incident took place in September 2024 , when PTI’s Ali Amin Gandapur was serving as the chief minister. Tarar went on to highlight that the KP government had not ensured the registration of all vehicles yet, as doing so makes the “surveillance of terrorists easier”. He added that potential revenue generated from car registration could have been used for the benefit of the people of KP. “You sacrificed the security of the entire province for your political gains. “You will now have to decide if you are with Pakistan or with Afghanistan. It is as clear as that,” the information minister declared. Reacting to the duo’s press conference, the PTI called for holding the federal and Punjab governments accountable, instead of levelling allegations against KP. In a statement , the party maintained that the information minister should explain on what basis he was labelling the entire provincial government as facilitators of terrorists, provided that the people of KP, police, security personnel, and political workers had made the “greatest” sacrifices in the war against terrorism. “Instead of political point-scoring, Attaullah Tarar should respect the blood of the martyrs,” it contended. “In such circumstances, it is a national responsibility for the federal minister to cooperate with the province instead of levelling accusations.” It urged Tarar to note the treatment facilities being provided under the PTI government’s Sehat Card programmes before lecturing the people of KP on health facilities. “Why has it not been possible to ensure the provision of quality and timely medical facilities to the people in Punjab as well?” the PTI asked. “Attaullah Tarar should also take a look at the state of affairs in Punjab,” it said, adding that 21pc of children aged 5 to 16 in Punjab were out of school according to a Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) report. Moreover, the PTI claimed that the farmers in Punjab were also forced to take to the streets to resolve their issues. Afghanistan’s ‘true face’ During his press conference, Tallal Chaudhry also highlighted the Afghan Taliban’s support for terrorist activities in Pakistan. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. The state minister noted that terrorist “proxies are financed by our eastern border and their hideouts are on the western border”. He emphasised that Islamabad had employed “every way” to convey its concerns to Kabul, including dialogue, dossiers and international forums, but to no avail. Referring to the recent attack on a rescue vehicle carrying DI Khan blast victims, Chaudhry said that attacking rescue teams was not allowed even during war. “This is their true face. Is this jihad? Even an enemy with some rules does not carry out such attacks.” He said such terrorist activities were carried out in exchange for receiving funds in dollars, which were proportional to the number of casualties. The interior official asserted that Pakistan had the “best systems” for investigating the identity of a suspected terrorist. “Very few countries have enough data that in less than a minute, any heinous crime or terrorist incident-related information can be accessed in Nadra and other databases […] we instantly find out whether they are Pakistanis [or not].” He then recalled that when authorities did not find any details in the database for a recent incident, they used open-source intelligence and geolocated a terrorist’s picture to Kabul’s Pashtunistan Square. September witnessed another bout of conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan, with the former saying it struck terrorist sites in the border region in response to a recent spate of terrorist attacks . Pakistan conducted “aerial and drone strikes” in another 10 locations across Afghanistan in retaliation for drones launched from across the border that were shot down in KP. The Foreign Office (FO) has said a demarche was also delivered to the Afghan side on Saturday on account of the Sept 23 airspace violation by drones.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs389.03 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs404.97 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Sept 29. The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Security forces kill 4 terrorists in Dera Ismail Khan IBO: state media. Security forces killed four terrorists during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Dera Ismail Khan on Monday, state-run APP reported citing sources. The report said the slain terrorists belonged to Fitna-al-Khawarij, a term the state uses for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. The sources said that the operation was conducted based on close intelligence-based surveillance of terrorist movements by the security forces, according to APP . A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was recovered from the terrorists, as well as Afghan currency, they added. KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. The province, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50pc, according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). More recently, on Saturday, a dozen people lost their lives while 35 others were injured in a suicide blast that targeted the Aman Mela police checkpost in DI Khan’s Darazinda tehsil. Earlier this month, police said they foiled an attack by TTP terrorists on a checkpost in DI Khan’s Daraban area. No casualties were reported among the police personnel. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation .

Israel security agency files complaint over report Netanyahu visited UAE. Israel’s domestic security service filed a complaint against a TV channel that reported Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited the UAE, his office said on Monday, the government’s first acknowledgement of the trip despite not naming the destination. “This evening the Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation,” read a statement from Netanyahu’s office, which oversees the security agency. On Sunday, Channel 12 and other Israeli media outlets reported that Netanyahu had visited the Gulf country to meet with President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Neither country has confirmed Netanyahu visited the UAE, with Monday’s statement the first acknowledgement of any kind by Israel. The visit came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the Emirati president had warned Netanyahu ahead of Hamas’s Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which the Israeli premier did not pass on to the security services. Netanyahu has denied the story. According to Israeli media, Netanyahu flew to the UAE on Sunday to ask Sheikh Mohamed to deny having given him that warning in 2023. The publication of his visit “endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad” spy agency and other top security officials, the PM’s office said in its statement. The visit was made public when the premier’s plane was still outside Israeli airspace, it noted. Mossad, which also operates under the prime minister’s office, issued a similar condemnation, according to the statement. Israel and the UAE formally established diplomatic relations in 2020 as part of the US-negotiated Abraham Accords.

Lahore police arrest key suspect in Azeri woman's gang-rape case. LAHORE: Police on Monday arrested one of the three suspects who allegedly gang-raped a foreign woman in Lahore. The 20-year-old Azeri woman had travelled to Pakistan for business purposes and was allegedly gang-raped by three men in a rented flat of a private housing society located near Raiwind on the night between Friday and Saturday. Lahore Deputy Inspector General (Investigation) Zeeshan Raza confirmed the arrest of the key suspect to Dawn , adding that two other suspects had also been identified and police teams were conducting raids to arrest them. “We are investigating the case in the light of the victim woman’s statement to the police,” he said. The official said that the woman’s medical report confirmed she was subjected to sexual assault. On Sunday, Lahore police requested federal authorities to place the names of the three prime suspects in the case on the Provisional National Identification List (PNIL), saying they had fled Lahore shortly after the alleged assault. Police had also taken two close relatives and a domestic servant of one of the suspects into custody. The vehicle allegedly used in the incident had also been taken into custody, he added. Woman records statement Earlier in the day, the Azeri woman recorded her statement under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before a judicial magistrate at the Cantonment Courts on Monday. The woman was brought to the court under tight security to record her statement before Judicial Magistrate Muhammad Sagheer. Before the proceedings began, the magistrate ordered all unrelated persons to leave the courtroom. The statement continued for more than an hour. The Defence C police had registered a case against three unidentified suspects on the woman’s complaint. It is the second such case in which a foreign woman was reportedly gang-raped in the Defence C police station area during the last four months. In June, two foreign women, nationals of the Netherlands and Venezuela, were allegedly abducted and sexually assaulted in the Defence C police station area. According to the FIR, the women were abducted by five suspects, including a close relative of a senior political personality, who demanded ransom and subjected them to sexual assault during their captivity.

No tax on factory to warehouse movements. ISLAMABAD: To curb harassment of taxpayers and streamline the movement of goods, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has announced that transferring goods from a factory to a registered person’s own warehouse under the same Sales Tax Registration Number (STRN) would not be treated as a taxable supply. As a result, inter-premises movement of goods also does not require the issuance of a digital invoice. However, consignments must be accompanied by a prescribed Stock Transfer Note (STN), clearly endorsed “Stock Transfer — Not a Taxable Supply”, in accordance with Sales Tax General Order No. 25 of 2026, issued on Monday. Under Section 2(33) of the Sales Tax Act 1990, a ‘supply’ requires a change of ownership or consideration. Since goods moving between a factory and warehouse of the same registrant involve no sale, they fall outside the charge of sales tax. However, where the receiving warehouse holds a separate STRN, the movement will be treated as a taxable supply, mandating issuance of digital invoicing and output tax. To prevent mischaracterisation during transit checks, the FBR has laid down detailed standard operating procedures (SOPs) governing the movement of goods between a factory and a registered person’s own warehouse, clarifying that such transfers are not taxable supplies. Federal Board of Revenue stops harassment of goods carriers As per SOPs, despatching units must generate a sequentially numbered Stock Transfer Note, endorsed prominently as “Stock Transfer — Not a Taxable Supply.” The value of goods is to be recorded strictly at cost for inventory control, without resembling a tax invoice. The STN must accompany consignments at all times during transit and be produced on demand at any checkpost. Upon receipt, the warehouse manager must acknowledge the consignment and update the warehouse stock register, while the factory must correspondingly update its own records under Rule 22. In case the receiving warehouse holds a separate STRN, the movement will be treated as a taxable supply. In such cases, the despatching unit must issue a digital invoice through the licensed integrator or PRAL, account for output tax, and reflect the transaction in the sales tax return. The STN procedure cannot substitute for invoicing in these circumstances. The order further instructs field formations not to treat an STN as noncompliance when both premises share the same STRN. Conversely, any consignment moving without either a tax invoice or a STN will be deemed prima facie undocumented and proceeded against under the law. The order also directs field formations to avoid unnecessary harassment. Officers are barred from demanding CNICs of drivers or detaining vehicles without proper cause. Goods in transit are not to be physically checked or unloaded, except for items listed in the Third Schedule, which may be inspected solely to verify retail price embossing. “Harassment of taxpayers, in any form or manner, is highly objectionable and shall not be tolerated,” the directive warns, adding that any departure from these instructions will be viewed seriously. Govt notifies new procurement rules with IMF team in town. • Changes retain certain exemptions for direct contracting with SOEs despite reservations • IMF delegation meets finance, tax officials amid uncertainty on sovereign wealth fund law ISLAMABAD: As question marks linger over the continuous breach of structural benchmarks regarding the sovereign wealth fund (SWF) law, the federal government on Monday notified new procurement rules two days ahead of the deadline, on the first day of talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for disbursement of $1.2 billion. Sources told Dawn that the IMF staff mission led by Iva Petrova held a series of discussions with officials from the finance ministry, the Federal Board of Revenue, the Establishment Division, and the finance secretaries of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab. The IMF team has been in Pakistan since September 23. It spent the initial days in Karachi for engagements with the State Bank of Pakistan and other stakeholders. The review talks usually begin with a customary call on the fina­nce minister, but he is currently abroad as part of the PM’s delegation to the UN General Assembly. The Sovereign Wealth Fund law is part of the discussions with the visiting IMF team. Authorities are in breach of an end-March 2026 structural benchmark on amendments to the Sovereign Wealth Fund Act to adopt governance mechanisms and safeguards for seven state-owned enterprises, involving an asset portfolio of about $8 billion. Most of them are blue-chip entities listed on the stock exchange but remain outside normal reporting requirements. They include OGDCL, PPL, Mari Petr­oleum, National Bank of Pakistan, Govt Holdings, Pakistan Development Fund, and the Neelum-Jhelum Hydropower project. The amendments are pending parliamentary approval. New procurement rules Against this backdrop, the government notified the Public Procurement Rules 2026 to promote greater transparency and competition in public procurement while keeping certain exemptions for direct contracting with SOEs and limiting the bidding to national firms. The IMF had certain reservations over the preferential treatment of SOEs for direct contracting. Rule 32 of the new rules provide that a procuring agency may engage through EPADS (E-Pak Acquisition and Disposal System, a digital system developed and enforced by the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority) to manage and administer the process of procurement in direct contracting with state-owned entities for the procurement of such works and services, including consultancy ser­vices, which are time-sensitive, scattered, remotely located and in the public interest or in case of urgency and provided they do not sub-let those contracts. The authorities would also have the powers in specific cases to limit bidding only to national bidders or certain categories of national bidders or prohibit participation of bidders of some nationalities or allow preference to domestic bidders for certain projects, and goods manufactured, mined, extracted and grown in the country. The Public Proc­urement Regulatory Authority (PPRA) said the new Public Proc­urement Rules 2026 repealed the Public Procurement Rules 2004. Made under Section 26 of the PPRA Ordinance 2002, the new rules have come into immediate effect, with procurement cases initiated prior to the commencement of the new rules continuing under the 2004 framework. The new rules make the use of EPADS mandatory for public procurement and disposal by federal procuring agencies, provide for the establishment of dedicated procurement cells, and introduce mechanisms to discourage conflicts of interest through third-party validation, evaluation, and pre-shipment inspection for large procurements. The new rules further strengthen the enforcement mechanism through the provision of blacklisting and cross-debarment, independent grievance red­ressal committees with an appellate mechanism at PPRA to clearly identify material deviations and mis-procurement, including deliberate procurement outside EPADS, failure to constitute prescribed committees, tailor-made specifications, violation of advertisement and response-time requirements, and failure to follow prescribed evaluation criteria. The rules allow other efficient methods of procurement such as gallop tendering and alternative procurement methods, including shopping and negotiated tendering, subject to specified conditions. Efficiency measures have been embedded in the framework, reducing response times, shortening standstill periods, and streamlining tender processing cycles to enable faster contract awards. The rules also emphasise sustainable procurement, encouraging inclusiveness of SMEs and marginalised groups, and aligning procurement practices with environmental policy. PPRA Managing Director Hasnat Ahmed Qureshi said new rules introduce a range of measures to strengthen oversight throughout the procurement cycle, from procurement planning and bidding to contract management, performance evaluation and closure. Security-development nexus. PAKISTAN can’t achieve sustained economic growth by treating security as a separate problem for the security apparatus to handle while econom­ists focus on investment, exports, productivity and fiscal reform. Insecurity destroys the very conditions on which economic development depe­nds, while development strengthens the foundations of security. Our crisis makes this nexus impossible to ignore. For decades, discussions on investment, production, growth, and development have largely focused on economic policies while underestimating the non-economic environment in which they operate. Yet, security of life and property, political stability, rule of law, judicial independence, federal-provincial coordination, accountability, and regional peace directly affect economic outcomes. Unless these improve, returns from economic reforms will remain below potential. Increasing militancy and Pakistan’s top position on the Global Terrorism Index 2026 are damaging lives and economic prospects. The recent attack on a police compound in Kohat, in which 37 people, including military personnel, were killed, received international coverage. Foreign business people and executives reportedly cancelled plan­ned visits, while travel advisories issued by sever­al governments can discourage their nationals from visiting Pakistan. In 2025, TTP attacks in KP and BLA strikes in Balochistan caused hundreds of ca­­sualties among security personnel. The past decade’s trend shows that terrorism is no longer episodic. It is a structural constraint on investment, trade, tourism, development and employment. The origins of the TTP challenge go back several decades. Pakistan’s decision in the 1980s to align with the US in opposing the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan had consequences beyond the immediate strategic goal. The proliferation of arms and drugs, sectarian violence, growth of militant groups and the spread of extremist ideologies created a social and institutional environment that facilitated terrorism in Pakistan. After the Soviets left Afghanistan, Pakistan became involved in efforts to shape a political settlement among Afghan factions. The failure of power-sharing arrangements and the ensuing civil war led to the emergence of the Taliban, who captured Kabul in 1996. Pakistan supported their regime. But 9/11 fundamentally altered the situation. Pakistan joined the global campaign against terrorism, itself becoming a major target. When the US decided to leave Afghanistan, Pakistan played an important role in the Doha process. The Ashraf Ghani government’s collapse in 2021 and the Taliban’s return led to expectations that cross-border terrorism would decline. Instead, the TTP, now equipped with modern weapons left behind by Nato forces, intensified their attacks. The challenge is to build security through development, and development through security. Diplomatic efforts involving China, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye have not produced a durable solution. Insecurity along the western frontier has disrupted bilateral trade, imposing costs on manufacturers, traders and transport operators, especially in KP and Balochistan. Security and commerce are now directly linked. Balochistan poses a different but equally serious challenge. It has seen a sharp escalation in asymmetric warfare and insurgency. Highways, railways, bridges, gas pipelines, electricity transmission lines, and other infrastructure have been targeted. Mine workers, labourers from other provinces and government officials have been attacked or abducted. In places, the state’s administrative presence and writ have been weakened. The economic consequences are immediate. Chi­­nese nationals and companies in Pakistan need extensive security. Attacks on Chinese citizens in Karachi, Dasu and elsewhere have led to concerns in Beijing and slowed some CPEC-related activities. Gwadar’s industrial potential remains largely unrealised, partly because Chinese companies are reluctant to deploy personnel in insecure conditions. An industrial zone won’t flourish when investors can’t operate confidently. Security operations alone can’t resolve Balochistan’s problem. Kinetic action is necessary against militants but must be accompanied by development. Balochistan suffers from serious deficits in education, health, clean water, infrastructure, employment and private investment. When economic opportunities are few, grievances become a source of recruitment for insurgent groups. So the province needs not just security spending but also a development strategy to create jobs, boost local institutions, and ensure communities see tangible benefits from Balochistan’s natural resources and strategic location. Regional instability adds to the problem. Disruption of trade with Iran and closure or restriction of border crossings such as Chaman have hurt exporters and communities that rely on cross-border commerce. Clearly, peace is not just a diplomatic aim; it is an economic asset. Pakistan must use its diplomatic capital to promote regional economic integration. Better ties with Afghanistan, structured dialogue with India, stable relations with Iran, and expanded links with Central Asian states can enlarge its economic space. Afghanistan, Iran, north India, and Central Asia can be important markets for Pakistani goods and services. Gwadar could become a transshipment and logistics gateway for landlocked Central Asian economies, generating transit revenues and creating opportunities for Pakistani exporters. Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan offer markets that Pakistan has so far penetrated modestly. Regional connectivity can revive projects such as the Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline, TAPI, and CASA, subject to their political, financial, commercial, and security feasibility. Greater regional trade will create demand for transport, logistics, warehousing, banking, insurance, IT and manufacturing. It will create jobs and give border communities greater economic sta­­ke in stability. None of this means that economic reforms should wait for peace. Quite the contrary. Fiscal reform, energy sector restructuring, taxation, deregulation, privatisation, export diversification, human capital development and institutional reform must continue uninterrupted. But they must be supported by steps that reduce the security premium imposed on economic activity. Security and development are two sides of the same national strategy. Insecurity raises transaction costs, discourages investment, destroys infrastructure, disrupts trade, deters foreign personnel and limits employment. Lack of economic opportunity, weak institutions and regional isolation can deepen the conditions in which insecurity flourishes. The goal should be to create an economy in which security, development and opportunity reinforce each other. Military capability can suppress threats. But only sustained economic development, effective institutions, political stability and regional peace can remove many of the conditions that allow those threats to regenerate. Our choice is not between security and development. The challenge is to build security through development, and development through security. Until that nexus becomes the organising principle of policy, economic reforms will operate below their potential and Pakistan will remain vulnerable to cycles of instability, low investment and weak growth. The writer is a former State Bank governor. Published in Dawn, September 29th, 2026

Off to elect another people. THE embattled prime minister of Israel has sworn to strip the citizenship of two Jewish filmmakers whose celebrated documentary has exposed the targeted genocide of Palestinian civilians carried out with impunity by the IDF. Journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have won standing ovations in the West for their film NAZA. The rule, Benjamin Netanyahu said, would apply to anyone who insults Israel’s military. Meanwhile, the fascism-hugging president of the US is busy doing what he can to try to strip those of citizenship and voting rights who are least likely to vote for his party. If he doesn’t win the midterms, he could be impeached. India’s ruling party, struggling to mask its old inspiration from the Nazis, has devised its own methods of stripping the citizenship rights of millions. According to a slew of reports, the BJP government is leaning on its chosen three-member election commission to deregister millions with a view to contriving state victories for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party. Bertolt Brecht’s satirical call to elect another people since the people had lost the confidence of the government has become ominously and palpably real. Coordinated moves by the three countries are linked by a quirk of fate in a post-Cold War bond. The rogue measures are not going unchallenged. A groundswell of protests primarily by students and unemployed youth is spreading across India against what reports have identified as the plundering of democracy in the country. New York’s Zohran Mamdani, Israel’s filmmakers and India’s Cockroach Janta Party are leading the pushback. The Indian protesters are directly accusing Modi’s handpicked three-member election commission of effectively changing poll verdicts, most recently in Bihar and West Bengal, by manipulating electoral rolls and surrendering the election commission’s neutral platform to the ruling party. The subversion is part of a global fraying of the lipstick on the pig, the ideological sleight of hand that was used to paint bourgeois democracies as enticing options against communist hardships. The moment the Soviet Union collapsed, however, the West’s definition of democracy itself took on a new life. It would henceforth be ‘free-market democracy’. Now that veneer, too, has blown away to herald raw plunder, assassinations, kidnappings and what leftist analysts have called ‘AI feudalism’. As the lipstick fades, big-power global rivalries deepen with unabashed candour. The West sought to keep up the pretence of supporting democracy, even though the fangs were out against elected and independent-minded leaders — for instance, in Iran in 1953 or Chile in 1973. Drooling at the promise of the American century, a clutch of former allies of the USSR were reduced to rubble. Yevgeny Primakov was the head of the KGB’s foreign intelligence unit when the USSR collapsed. He became Russia’s foreign minister and subsequently rose to become prime minister. Primakov moved to staunch the Russian haemorrhage caused by the chasm between Mikhail Gorbachev and Boris Yeltsin. The Russia-India-China (RIC) grouping was his brainchild, but he was already late since the US-Israel-India group was installed more swiftly. For Indian ideologues, who were regarded as Western catspaws during the Cold War, the alignment with Israel under the false pretence of democratic camaraderie was a windfall. The BJP gained most from the turn of events, though the Congress had its own pro-West ideologues licking their chops. As the lipstick fades, big-power global rivalries deepen with unabashed candour. As capitalism struggled to breathe sans the Red Terror as its ruse, the fangs could barely be hidden. During the Cold War (roughly 1945-1991), capitalist democracies — particularly in Western Europe and North America — faced a powerful ideological rival in global communism. To prove that capitalism was the superior system for the working class, many Western nations built robust welfare states. They invested heavily in public healthcare and education, strong labour unions and worker protections, high progressive taxation to fund social safety nets, and affordable housing and infrastructure. Most analysts have concluded that the systemic threat of communism acted as a ‘regulatory check’ on raw capitalism, forcing it to present a more compassionate, egalitarian face to prevent domestic socialist revolutions. Once the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, critics and economists argue, this pressure disappeared. With no competing global model, a more aggressive, unregulated version of capitalism led by neoliberalism gained dominant global traction. Whether it involves winning elections by waging brutal wars or carrying out genocide, or stripping voters of their rights, the trigger is capitalism’s inability to leave its fate to the voting masses. While democracy promises power to the many, its mechanisms can be co-opted by the few to maintain control. Some regimes maintain the outward appearance of democracy — such as holding regular elections — while systematically eroding democratic institutions from within. This dynamic is often referred to as a ‘hybrid regime’ or ‘competitive authoritarianism’. Ruling elites use legal frameworks, regulatory bodies, and gerrymandering to tilt the playing field in their favour, making it incredibly difficult for opposition forces to compete fairly. It’s evident in India, as in the US or Israel — the post-Cold War ‘democratic allies’ — that campaign financing, lobbying, and the influence of wealthy donors mean that policy decisions really reflect the interests of economic elites rather than those of the average voter. All three countries have used religion to manufacture consent. This is beginning to create a disconnect in which citizens feel their vote carries no real weight in policy outcomes. The Jantar Mantar protests in Delhi are a clear aspect of this churning. The protesters are well aware that elites consolidate control over media landscapes or leverage algorithms and disinformation to shape public perception. By controlling the narrative, they can manufacture consent or distract the public from systemic issues. Donald Trump’s threat from the UN platform to murder 91 million Iranians, and the Indian election commission’s removal of 130m names from electoral rolls in the last nine months, are shared responses to their fraying economies’ growing need to dump democratic pretence all over again. Pakistani women face highest heart disease mortality in South Asia, study finds. KARACHI: Pakistani women have the highest death rate from ischaemic heart disease among five South Asian countries, with high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity and physical inactivity identified as factors increasing their risk, health experts said on Monday. On the eve of World Heart Day, cardiologists, gynaecologists and local industry leaders gathered at the Karachi Press Club (KPC) to announce the launch of a nationwide ‘Her Heart Matters’ campaign. The campaign was launched by PharmEvo in collaboration with the Pakistan Cardiac Society, the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Pakistan, the Pakistan Society of Internal Medicine, and Go Red for Women to promote screening, awareness and education for early detection and timely treatment of cardiovascular risks. The experts said that a 2026 study published in JACC: Asia compared Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan using Global Burden of Disease estimates. On the eve of World Heart Day, experts call for greater screening and follow-up as hypertension, diabetes, obesity and physical inactivity raise cardiovascular risks among women The study found that Pakistan had the highest age-standardised death rate from ischaemic heart disease among women in the five countries in 2021. Pakistan was also the only country studied where the ratio of deaths to estimated cases was higher among women than men, at 4.4 per cent compared with 3.1pc. High blood pressure and diets low in vegetables and fibre were identified as leading contributors to heart disease deaths among Pakistani women. The experts, speaking at a press conference at KPC, said heart disease among women was often ignored due to misconceptions that it mainly affected men, inadequate screening and poor follow-up during pregnancy, after childbirth and after menopause. Prof Dr Tazeen Abbas, secretary general of the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Pakistan, said women’s heart health needed attention before and during pregnancy, after childbirth and after menopause. She said many women stopped prescribed medicines during pregnancy or discontinued blood-pressure treatment after delivery, and should instead consult their doctors. High blood pressure during pregnancy was often forgotten after childbirth, she said, and pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy, in which the heart muscle weakens around pregnancy, could be serious if not treated in time. Prof Dr Halima Yasmeen, chairperson and head of department at Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC), said heart disease had been detected in around four per cent of pregnant women screened at her clinic. Prof Dr Shabnam Naveed, head of medicine at JPMC and Jinnah Sindh Medical University, said more than 90pc of women attending JPMC’s diabetes clinic had one or more cardiovascular risk factors. Though a high-risk hospital group, the figure showed the close link between diabetes, hypertension, obesity and heart disease, she added, and lack of screening remained a barrier. Prof Dr Fawad Farooq, general secretary of the Pakistan Cardiac Society, said stress was another important contributor to cardiovascular disease. Women could add walking and other physical activities to their routines even with limited space or time, he added. He said specialised cardiac hospitals were receiving large numbers of patients with heart attacks and chest pain because “Pakistan lacked an effective primary and secondary cardiovascular care network”. “At the NICVD, spaces meant for one patient sometimes have to accommodate several patients, while multiple heart-attack patients can arrive at the same time,” Prof Farooq said, adding that tertiary hospitals alone could not manage Pakistan’s growing cardiovascular burden. He said some patients stopped taking prescribed medicines within weeks of undergoing angioplasty, exposing themselves to further complications. Stronger primary care, proper follow-up and continued use of medicines were necessary to prevent repeat heart attacks and reduce pressure on specialised hospitals. Dr Mansoor Ahmed, Professor of Cardiology at the Karachi Institute of Heart Diseases, said the longstanding belief that women did not develop heart disease had been proved wrong. He said heart disease affected women as well as men, but Pakistani women often placed their own health behind household responsibilities. Families also failed to give adequate attention to women’s medical needs, while limited physical activity was increasing their risk. He added that diabetes had become a major public health problem in Pakistan and frequently occurred alongside cardiovascular disease. “Women living with diabetes, high blood pressure or obesity require regular screening to identify heart disease before serious complications develop,” he said.
